different stages of syphilis particularly as a manifestation of late/congenital syphilis **Etiology** Causative organism
- Treponema pallidum Transmission
- Sexual transmission
- Congenital transmission from infected mother to fetus **Types of Joint Involvement** 1 Acute syphilitic arthritis May occur during secondary syphilis 2 Chronic syphilitic arthropathy May occur in late disease 3 Charcot arthropathy A neuropathic arthropathy associated with tabes dorsalis a late neurological manifestation of syphilis 4 Congenital syphilitic skeletal disease May affect ◦ Long bones ◦ Joints ◦ Epiphyses/metaphyses **Pathophysiology** Treponema pallidum infection ↓ Systemic infection ↓ Inflammatory response ↓ Synovial and periarticular involvement ↓ Chronic tissue damage In late neurosyphilis Dorsal column sensory loss ↓ Loss of proprioception and protective sensation ↓ Repetitive joint trauma ↓ Progressive neuropathic arthropathy ↓ Joint destruction and deformity **Clinical Features** **Acute syphilitic arthritis**
- Joint pain
- Joint swelling
- Stiffness
- Effusion
- Restricted movement
- May involve multiple joints
- Constitutional symptoms may occur **Chronic syphilitic arthropathy**
- Chronic joint pain or discomfort
- Swelling
- Progressive deformity
- Restricted movement **Charcot joint** Characteristic features
- Recurrent painless or relatively painless trauma
- Swelling
- Warmth
- Deformity
- Crepitus
- Subluxation/dislocation
- Severe radiological destruction
- The knee and hip can be affected among other joints **Investigations** **Serological tests** Non treponemal tests
- VDRL
- RPR Treponemal tests
- TPHA/TPPA
- FTA ABS or equivalent treponemal assays **Joint investigations**
- Joint aspiration when indicated
- Synovial fluid analysis
- Culture to exclude pyogenic infection **Imaging**
- X ray
- MRI when required **Neurological evaluation** If Charcot arthropathy is suspected
- Sensory examination
- Proprioception
- Reflexes
- Neurological assessment **Differential Diagnosis**
- Rheumatoid arthritis
- Osteoarthritis
- Septic arthritis
- Tuberculous arthritis
- Gout
- Neuropathic arthropathy due to other causes **Complications**
- Joint destruction
- Deformity
- Subluxation
- Dislocation
- Pathological fracture
- Instability
- Loss of function
- Secondary osteoarthritis
- Neurological disability in associated neurosyphilis **Medical Management** Specific treatment Penicillin based therapy is the standard treatment for syphilis with the exact preparation dose and duration determined by the stage and clinical form of disease Management may include
- Appropriate penicillin therapy
- Treatment of sexual partners according to public health guidance
- Screening for other sexually transmitted infections
- Neurological evaluation when indicated
- Analgesics
- Management of secondary complications **For Charcot arthropathy**
- Protection from excessive loading
- Off loading
- Appropriate orthosis
- Footwear modification where applicable
- Management of associated neurological disease **Surgical Management** Surgery is generally directed toward the resulting structural damage rather than eradication of the infection itself May include
- Synovectomy in selected cases
- Debridement when indicated
- Arthrodesis for severe instability
- Joint reconstruction
- Joint replacement in selected patients after appropriate infection treatment
- Correction of severe deformity **Rehabilitation**
- Protection of affected joint
- Pain management
- Maintaining safe ROM
- Muscle strengthening
- Orthotic support
- Gait training
- Assistive devices when required
- Patient education regarding joint protection/////////// 

**1 OSTEOMA DEFINITION** Osteoma is a benign slow growing tumour composed of mature compact or cancellous bone It commonly occurs in the skull and facial bones and rarely causes malignant transformation **CLASSIFICATION According to site** Central osteoma Develops within bone Peripheral osteoma Develops from the surface of bone **According to structure** Compact osteoma Cancellous osteoma **ETIOLOGY** The exact cause is uncertain Possible factors
- Developmental abnormality
- Genetic factors
- Previous trauma
- Chronic irritation
- Associated syndromes particularly Gardner syndrome **CLINICAL FEATURES** Small osteomas may be asymptomatic When symptomatic
- Slow growing hard swelling
- Painless mass
- Facial asymmetry
- Headache in some cranial lesions
- Sinus obstruction
- Visual symptoms if orbital structures are involved
- Cosmetic deformity **INVESTIGATIONS**
- X ray Dense well defined bony lesion
- CT scan Best for defining the size location and relationship to surrounding structures
- MRI Useful when soft tissue or intracranial involvement is suspected
- Biopsy Usually not required for a typical small osteoma but may be performed when diagnosis is uncertain **COMPLICATIONS**
- Cosmetic deformity
- Pressure on adjacent structures
- Sinus obstruction
- Visual impairment
- Rare neurological complications
- Recurrence after incomplete excision **MEDICAL MANAGEMENT**
- Asymptomatic Observation Periodic clinical/imaging follow up
- Symptomatic Analgesics for pain Treatment of associated sinus symptoms **SURGICAL MANAGEMENT** Indications Pain Functional impairment Significant cosmetic deformity Rapid or uncertain growth Compression of adjacent structures Procedure Complete surgical excision is the treatment of choice for symptomatic lesions **PROGNOSIS** Osteoma is benign and usually has an excellent prognosis Recurrence is uncommon after complete excision --- 

**2 OSTEOSARCOMA DEFINITION** Osteosarcoma is a malignant primary bone tumour in which the malignant tumour cells produce osteoid or immature bone It is the most common primary malignant bone tumour in many clinical series particularly among adolescents **CLASSIFICATION** 1 Conventional high grade osteosarcoma
- Osteoblastic
- Chondroblastic
- Fibroblastic 2 Other types
- Telangiectatic osteosarcoma
- Parosteal osteosarcoma
- Periosteal osteosarcoma
- Secondary osteosarcoma **COMMON SITES** Usually occurs in the metaphysis of long bones Common sites
- Lower end of femur
- Upper end of tibia
- Upper end of humerus **ETIOLOGY / RISK FACTORS** Exact cause is unknown Risk factors
- Previous radiotherapy
- Paget disease of bone
- Hereditary retinoblastoma
- Li Fraumeni syndrome
- Certain
genetic abnormalities
- Rapid skeletal growth may be associated with adolescent presentation **PATHOPHYSIOLOGY** Malignant transformation of osteogenic cells ↓ Rapid tumour growth ↓ Production of malignant osteoid ↓ Destruction of normal bone ↓ Extension into soft tissues ↓ Blood borne metastasis Most commonly lungs **CLINICAL FEATURES** Local
- Progressive bone pain initially intermittent later persistent
- Swelling and tenderness
- Reduced movement of adjacent joint
- Limp if lower limb is affected Advanced
- Large hard mass
- Venous congestion
- Pathological fracture
- Severe functional limitation Systemic Systemic symptoms may be absent initially **INVESTIGATIONS**
- X ray May show mixed lytic and sclerotic lesion cortical destruction periosteal reaction sunburst appearance Codmans triangle
- MRI Important for local tumour extent neurovascular involvement soft tissue extension surgical planning
- CT chest Used to assess pulmonary metastases
- Bone scan / PET CT May be used for staging
- Biopsy Definitive diagnosis requires appropriate tumour biopsy planned so that the biopsy tract can be removed during definitive surgery **COMPLICATIONS**
- Pathological fracture
- Local tissue destruction
- Neurovascular involvement
- Pulmonary metastasis
- Bone metastases
- Recurrence
- Death if untreated **MEDICAL MANAGEMENT** Osteosarcoma is usually treated using multimodal therapy
- Chemotherapy Usually given before surgery neoadjuvant chemotherapy and after surgery adjuvant chemotherapy Common agents may include combinations containing High dose methotrexate Doxorubicin Cisplatin
- Supportive management Analgesics Nutritional support Psychological support Management of chemotherapy complications **SURGICAL MANAGEMENT**
- Limb salvage surgery Preferred when adequate oncological margins can be achieved while preserving useful limb function May involve wide excision endoprosthetic reconstruction structural bone grafting in selected cases
- Amputation Considered when limb salvage cannot achieve adequate tumour control major neurovascular involvement prevents safe resection or extensive local disease makes reconstruction unsuitable **PHYSIOTHERAPY**
- Preoperative Maintain ROM Maintain muscle strength Pain management Psychological preparation
- Postoperative Wound and limb protection Gradual ROM Strengthening Prosthetic training if amputation is performed Gait training Functional rehabilitation **PROGNOSIS** Prognosis depends on Tumour size Site Presence of metastasis Response to chemotherapy Surgical margins --- 

**3 OSTEOCHONDROMA DEFINITION** Osteochondroma is a benign bone forming tumour characterized by a cartilage capped bony projection that arises from the surface of bone and typically contains cortex and medulla continuous with the underlying bone It is the most common benign bone tumour **TYPES**
- Solitary osteochondroma
- Multiple hereditary osteochondromas also called hereditary multiple exostoses **COMMON SITES** Usually near the metaphysis of long bones Distal femur Proximal tibia Proximal humerus **ETIOLOGY** Usually developmental Genetic mutations involving the EXT gene family are important in hereditary multiple osteochondromas **CLINICAL FEATURES** Many are asymptomatic Symptoms include
- Painless bony swelling
- Cosmetic deformity
- Mechanical irritation
- Pain due to pressure on surrounding structures
- Restricted movement
- Limb length discrepancy
- Nerve compression
- Vascular compression **INVESTIGATIONS**
- X ray Characteristic bony projection from cortex medullary continuity with parent bone
- CT Useful for complex anatomical areas
- MRI Useful to evaluate cartilage cap neurovascular structures suspicious malignant transformation **COMPLICATIONS**
- Mechanical irritation
- Fracture of stalk
- Nerve compression
- Vascular compression
- Deformity
- Limb length discrepancy
- Rare malignant transformation into secondary chondrosarcoma **MEDICAL MANAGEMENT**
- Asymptomatic Observation Periodic review
- Symptomatic Analgesics Activity modification Physiotherapy for secondary functional problems **SURGICAL MANAGEMENT** Excision is indicated for Pain Functional impairment Neurovascular compression Significant deformity Suspicion of malignant transformation Growth after skeletal maturity Complete excision usually provides excellent results --- 

**4 ENCHONDROMA DEFINITION** Enchondroma is a benign cartilage forming tumour that develops within the medullary cavity of bone **COMMON SITES** Small bones of hands Feet Femur Humerus Tibia **ETIOLOGY** Usually sporadic Multiple enchondromas may occur in Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome **CLINICAL FEATURES** Often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally Symptoms include
- Local swelling
- Pain
- Pathological fracture
- Deformity
- Reduced function Note Pain in an otherwise uncomplicated lesion requires evaluation for other causes including possible malignant transformation **INVESTIGATIONS**
- X ray May show well defined intramedullary lucent lesion scattered calcifications cortical thinning endosteal scalloping
- MRI Useful to assess cartilage characteristics soft tissue extension aggressive features
- CT Useful for mineralization and cortical assessment
- Biopsy Required when imaging is atypical or malignancy is suspected **COMPLICATIONS**
- Pathological fracture
- Deformity
- Recurrence
- Rare malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma
- Increased risk of malignancy in some multiple lesion syndromes **MANAGEMENT**
- Asymptomatic Observation Periodic clinical/imaging follow up
- Symptomatic Curettage Bone grafting or suitable cavity filling when indicated Internal fixation if required for structural stability
- Malignant transformation Wide surgical excision according to tumour grade and location --- 

**5 EWINGS SARCOMA DEFINITION** Ewing sarcoma is a malignant small round cell tumour of bone or soft tissue most commonly affecting children and adolescents It is associated with characteristic genetic alterations classically involving EWSR1 most often through an EWSR1 FLI1 fusion **COMMON SITES** Pelvis Femur Tibia Fibula Ribs Humerus Vertebrae **ETIOLOGY** The exact cause is unknown Genetic translocations are
characteristic **PATHOPHYSIOLOGY** Malignant cellular proliferation ↓ Bone marrow involvement ↓ Cortical destruction ↓ Periosteal reaction ↓ Soft tissue extension ↓ Metastasis Lungs Bone Bone marrow **CLINICAL FEATURES**
- Bone pain Swelling Tenderness
- Fever Malaise Weight loss
- Reduced function Limp
- Pathological fracture Because fever and inflammatory markers can be prominent it may initially resemble infection **INVESTIGATIONS**
- Blood CBC ESR/CRP LDH may have prognostic relevance
- X ray Classically permeative/moth eaten destruction lamellated or onion skin periosteal reaction
- MRI Defines local extent soft tissue involvement neurovascular relationship
- CT chest Pulmonary staging
- PET CT / Bone marrow assessment May be used according to staging protocol
- Biopsy Required for definitive diagnosis **COMPLICATIONS**
- Pathological fracture Local tissue destruction
- Pulmonary metastasis Bone metastasis Bone marrow involvement
- Recurrence Treatment related complications **MEDICAL MANAGEMENT** Ewing sarcoma is treated with systemic chemotherapy plus local control Chemotherapy may include multi agent regimens such as Vincristine Doxorubicin Cyclophosphamide Ifosfamide Etoposide exact regimen depends on contemporary oncology protocols **SURGICAL MANAGEMENT AND RADIOTHERAPY**
- Surgery Wide local excision Limb salvage surgery Reconstruction Amputation in selected cases
- Radiotherapy Ewing sarcoma is relatively radiosensitive and radiotherapy may be used when surgery cannot achieve adequate margins tumour is unresectable local control is otherwise inadequate or in selected high risk situations --- 

**6 GIANT CELL TUMOUR OF BONE DEFINITION** Giant cell tumour GCT of bone is a generally benign but locally aggressive bone tumour composed of mononuclear stromal cells and numerous osteoclast like giant cells It can rarely metastasize particularly to the lungs **AGE** Usually occurs in young adults most commonly between skeletal maturity and approximately 40 years **COMMON SITES** Lower end of femur Upper end of tibia Distal radius Proximal humerus It characteristically involves the epiphysis extending to the subarticular bone **CLINICAL FEATURES**
- Pain Progressive swelling Tenderness
- Joint stiffness Reduced joint movement
- Pathological fracture **INVESTIGATIONS**
- X ray Typical eccentric lytic lesion expansile lesion soap bubble appearance little or no matrix mineralization extension to subchondral bone
- MRI Determines soft tissue extension relationship with neurovascular structures surgical planning
- Biopsy Required for definitive diagnosis
- Chest imaging May be performed because rare pulmonary metastases can occur **COMPLICATIONS**
- Pathological fracture
- Joint destruction
- Local recurrence
- Secondary osteoarthritis
- Rare pulmonary metastasis
- Rare malignant transformation **MEDICAL MANAGEMENT** Selected cases may be treated with Denosumab particularly when surgery would cause unacceptable morbidity or in selected unresectable/recurrent disease Pain management and supportive care **SURGICAL MANAGEMENT**
- Extended curettage Often combined with high speed burring local adjuvants bone graft/cement filling
- Wide excision Considered for extensive soft tissue extension recurrent disease destructive lesions selected aggressive tumours
- Reconstruction Bone graft Cement Prosthetic reconstruction Arthroplasty where indicated --- 

**7 MULTIPLE MYELOMA DEFINITION** Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell disorder characterized by clonal proliferation of plasma cells in bone marrow production of a monoclonal immunoglobulin or light chain and characteristic bone destruction anemia renal dysfunction and hypercalcemia **PATHOPHYSIOLOGY** Clonal plasma cell proliferation ↓ Bone marrow infiltration ↓ Osteoclast activation + osteoblast suppression ↓ Osteolytic bone lesions ↓ Hypercalcemia + pathological fractures **COMMON SITES** Vertebrae Ribs Skull Pelvis Proximal femur Proximal humerus **CLINICAL FEATURES** Mnemonic CRAB
- C HyperCalcemia Nausea Constipation Confusion Excessive thirst
- R Renal impairment Reduced renal function
- A Anemia Fatigue Weakness Pallor
- B Bone lesions Bone pain Pathological fractures Vertebral collapse Reduced height Other features Recurrent infections Weight loss Neurological symptoms due to vertebral collapse **INVESTIGATIONS**
- Blood CBC Serum calcium Renal function Total protein Serum protein electrophoresis Immunofixation Serum free light chains
- Urine Urine protein electrophoresis/immunofixation Bence Jones protein/light chains
- Bone marrow Bone marrow aspiration/biopsy
- Imaging Low dose whole body CT MRI PET CT where appropriate **COMPLICATIONS**
- Pathological fractures Vertebral collapse Spinal cord compression
- Hypercalcemia Renal failure Severe anemia Recurrent infections
- Amyloidosis Thrombosis **MEDICAL MANAGEMENT** Treatment is hematology/oncology directed May include
- Combination anti myeloma therapy Proteasome inhibitors Immunomodulatory drugs Monoclonal antibodies Corticosteroids
- Bisphosphonates or denosumab in appropriate patients
- Radiotherapy for selected painful/local lesions

- Supportive treatment Hydration Management of hypercalcemia Renal support Treatment of anemia Infection prevention/treatment Pain management **SURGICAL MANAGEMENT** Surgery is mainly for complications Stabilization of pathological fractures Vertebral augmentation in selected cases Spinal decompression/stabilization for neurological compromise Fixation of impending or established fractures --- 

**8 METASTATIC BONE TUMOURS DEFINITION** Metastatic bone tumour is a malignant tumour in bone that has spread from a primary malignant tumour located elsewhere in the body It is more common than primary malignant bone tumours **COMMON PRIMARY TUMOURS** Breast Prostate Lung Kidney Thyroid **TYPES**
- Osteolytic metastases Cause bone destruction Commonly Renal cell carcinoma Lung carcinoma Thyroid carcinoma
- Osteoblastic metastases Cause increased bone formation/sclerosis Classically Prostate carcinoma

- Biopsy May be required if primary tumour is unknown imaging is atypical or histological confirmation is required before treatment **COMPLICATIONS**

- Severe pain Paralysis Reduced mobility Hypercalcemic crisis Death from primary malignancy **MEDICAL MANAGEMENT** Management depends on the primary cancer May include Systemic anticancer therapy Hormonal therapy Chemotherapy Targeted therapy Immunotherapy Bisphosphonates Denosumab Analgesics Radiotherapy Particularly useful for painful metastases local tumour control spinal cord compression in selected circumstances **SURGICAL MANAGEMENT** Indications Pathological fracture Impending fracture Spinal instability Neurological compression Severe mechanical pain Procedures Internal fixation Intramedullary nailing Plate fixation Endoprosthetic reconstruction Spinal decompression and stabilization 

**PART B HIP AND AVASCULAR CONDITIONS** --- 

**9 PERTHES DISEASE DEFINITION** Legg Calve Perthes disease is a childhood disorder characterized by idiopathic avascular necrosis of the developing femoral head followed by fragmentation reossification and remodeling **AGE** Usually 4 10 years More common in boys **ETIOLOGY** The exact cause is unknown Possible factors Temporary interruption of blood supply Genetic predisposition Coagulation abnormalities Environmental factors Repeated microtrauma **PATHOPHYSIOLOGY** Interruption of blood supply ↓ Femoral head ischemia ↓ Bone necrosis ↓ Fragmentation ↓ Revascularization ↓ Reossification ↓ Remodeling **STAGES** 1 Initial/necrosis stage 2 Fragmentation stage 3 Reossification stage 4 Healed/remodeling stage **CLINICAL FEATURES**
- Limp Hip pain Groin pain Referred knee pain
- Reduced hip ROM Restricted abduction Restricted internal rotation
- Muscle wasting Trendelenburg gait **INVESTIGATIONS**
- X ray May show increased density of femoral head flattening fragmentation subchondral fracture loss of sphericity
- MRI Can detect early disease before X ray changes **COMPLICATIONS**
- Femoral head deformity Coxa magna Coxa plana Subluxation
- Leg length discrepancy Early osteoarthritis Chronic hip pain Reduced hip function **MEDICAL/CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT** Goals Maintain hip mobility Maintain femoral head containment Reduce mechanical stress Prevent deformity Methods Activity modification Avoid high impact activities Analgesics/NSAIDs when appropriate Physiotherapy ROM exercises particularly abduction and internal rotation Traction in selected cases Bracing/containment treatment in selected patients **SURGICAL MANAGEMENT** Indications Depend on age femoral head involvement loss of containment progressive deformity Procedures Femoral varus osteotomy Pelvic osteotomy Other containment procedures **PHYSIOTHERAPY** Gentle ROM Hip abduction exercises Muscle strengthening Hydrotherapy where appropriate Gait training Avoid excessive impact Maintain functional independence --- 

**10 SLIPPED CAPITAL FEMORAL EPIPHYSIS SCFE DEFINITION** Slipped capital femoral epiphysis SCFE is a disorder of adolescence in which the proximal femoral epiphysis slips relative to the femoral neck through the growth plate usually producing posteromedial displacement of the epiphysis relative to the metaphysis **AGE AND RISK FACTORS** Age Commonly 10 16 years often during the adolescent growth spurt More common in boys Risk Factors Obesity Rapid growth Endocrine disorders Hypothyroidism Growth hormone abnormalities Renal disease Previous radiotherapy **CLASSIFICATION**
- Stable SCFE Patient can walk with or without crutches
- Unstable SCFE Patient cannot walk even with assistance Higher risk of avascular necrosis **CLINICAL FEATURES**
- Hip pain Groin pain Thigh pain Referred knee pain Limp
- Reduced hip movement
- Characteristic finding During passive hip flexion the hip may move into external rotation
- Shortened affected limb External rotation deformity Limited internal rotation Difficulty walking **INVESTIGATIONS**
- X ray AP pelvis Frog leg lateral for stable cases avoid forced positioning in suspected unstable SCFE May show widened physis displacement of epiphysis Kleins line abnormality
- MRI Useful in early/pre slip cases when radiographs are inconclusive **COMPLICATIONS**
- Avascular necrosis of femoral head Chondrolysis Femoroacetabular impingement
- Premature osteoarthritis Limb deformity Leg length discrepancy **MEDICAL MANAGEMENT** SCFE requires urgent orthopaedic management Until definitive treatment Stop weight bearing Bed/rest or protected mobility Analgesia Avoid forceful hip manipulation **SURGICAL MANAGEMENT** Standard treatment is in situ fixation especially for stable slips e g percutaneous screw fixation For selected severe/ unstable slips more extensive corrective procedures may be considered Prophylactic fixation of contralateral hip may be considered in high risk patients **PHYSIOTHERAPY** After surgical stabilization Protected weight bearing as prescribed ROM exercises as allowed Progressive strengthening Gait training Functional rehabilitation Weight management and activity modification --- 

**11 AVASCULAR NECROSIS OF BONE DEFINITION** Avascular necrosis AVN is the death of bone tissue caused by loss or significant reduction of its blood supply The femoral head is a common site **CAUSES**
- Traumatic Femoral neck fracture Hip dislocation
- Non traumatic Long term corticosteroid use Excessive alcohol use Sickle cell disease Certain autoimmune diseases Radiation Caisson disease Hypercoagulable states Some metabolic disorders Idiopathic **PATHOPHYSIOLOGY** Reduced blood supply ↓ Ischemia ↓ Death of osteocytes ↓ Structural weakening ↓ Subchondral fracture ↓ Collapse of bone ↓ Secondary osteoarthritis **CLINICAL FEATURES**
- Early May be asymptomatic
Mild hip/groin pain
- Progressive Deep hip pain Pain on weight bearing Pain at rest in advanced disease Restricted ROM Limp Difficulty climbing stairs Difficulty walking **INVESTIGATIONS**
- X ray May be normal in early disease Later Sclerosis Cystic changes Crescent sign Femoral head collapse Secondary osteoarthritis
- MRI Most sensitive investigation for early AVN
- CT Useful for assessing structural collapse **COMPLICATIONS**
- Femoral head collapse Secondary osteoarthritis Severe pain
- Reduced mobility Leg length discrepancy Joint stiffness Disability **MEDICAL MANAGEMENT** Depends on stage Activity modification Protected weight bearing Analgesics/NSAIDs Treatment of underlying cause reduction/discontinuation of causative drugs only under medical supervision Management of associated metabolic conditions Note No medical treatment reliably reverses established femoral head collapse **SURGICAL MANAGEMENT**
- Early disease Core decompression Bone grafting in selected cases Joint preserving procedures
- Advanced disease Total hip arthroplasty if significant collapse and arthritis are present **PHYSIOTHERAPY** Pain relieving modalities as appropriate Protected weight bearing ROM exercises Strengthening Gait training Assistive devices Postoperative rehabilitation after arthroplasty 

**PART C METABOLIC BONE DISEASES** --- 

**12 RICKETS DEFINITION** Rickets is a disorder of the growing skeleton caused by defective mineralization of the growth plate and newly formed bone most commonly due to vitamin D deficiency or impaired vitamin D metabolism **CAUSES**
- Nutritional Vitamin D deficiency Calcium deficiency Phosphate deficiency
- Malabsorption Chronic gastrointestinal disease Malabsorption syndromes
- Renal Chronic kidney disease Renal tubular disorders
- Genetic Hereditary vitamin D dependent rickets Hypophosphatemic rickets **PATHOPHYSIOLOGY** Vitamin D / calcium / phosphate deficiency ↓ Reduced mineralization ↓ Defective growth plate mineralization ↓ Bone deformity and weakness ↓ Skeletal abnormalities **CLINICAL FEATURES** General Growth retardation Irritability Muscle weakness Delayed development Skeletal Frontal bossing Craniotabes in infants Delayed closure of fontanelle Rachitic rosary Harrison sulcus Pigeon chest Widening of wrists and ankles Bow legs Knock knees Spinal deformity Dental Delayed dentition Enamel defects **INVESTIGATIONS**
- Blood Serum calcium Phosphate ALP 25 hydroxyvitamin D PTH Renal function when indicated
- X ray Typical metaphyseal widening cupping fraying splaying reduced bone density **COMPLICATIONS**
- Skeletal deformity Growth retardation Fractures
- Muscle weakness Delayed motor development Hypocalcemic seizures in severe cases Dental abnormalities **MEDICAL MANAGEMENT**
- Nutritional rickets Vitamin D supplementation Adequate calcium intake Adequate phosphate where required Balanced diet Safe sunlight exposure
- Specific forms Treatment directed at underlying cause e g Phosphate supplementation for hypophosphatemic disorders Active vitamin D analogues in appropriate disorders **SURGICAL MANAGEMENT** Usually unnecessary if treated early May be required for severe residual deformity or persistent angular deformity Procedures Guided growth Corrective osteotomy --- 

**13 OSTEOMALACIA DEFINITION** Osteomalacia is a disorder of adults characterized by defective mineralization of newly formed bone most commonly due to vitamin D deficiency or impaired vitamin D metabolism Difference Rickets affects the growing skeleton and growth plates osteomalacia affects mature bone **CAUSES** Vitamin D deficiency Calcium deficiency Malabsorption Chronic kidney disease Liver disease affecting vitamin D metabolism Anticonvulsant medications Phosphate wasting disorders **PATHOPHYSIOLOGY** Vitamin D deficiency / impaired mineral metabolism ↓ Reduced calcium/phosphate availability ↓ Defective mineralization ↓ Accumulation of osteoid ↓ Soft and weak bones **CLINICAL FEATURES**
- Diffuse bone pain Bone tenderness
- Proximal muscle weakness Difficulty climbing stairs Difficulty rising from a chair
- Waddling gait Fractures or pseudofractures Fatigue **INVESTIGATIONS**
- Blood Calcium Phosphate ALP 25 hydroxyvitamin D PTH Renal function
- X ray May show reduced bone density Looser zones/pseudofractures
- Bone density May show reduced BMD but does not by itself distinguish osteomalacia from osteoporosis **COMPLICATIONS**
- Pathological fractures Pseudofractures Skeletal deformity
- Chronic pain Muscle weakness Falls Functional disability **MEDICAL MANAGEMENT** Vitamin D replacement Calcium supplementation Correction of phosphate deficiency where applicable Treatment of underlying malabsorption/renal disease Nutritional correction **SURGICAL MANAGEMENT AND PHYSIOTHERAPY** Surgery Generally not required May be needed for severe deformity or complicated fractures Physiotherapy Muscle strengthening Balance training Gait training Fall prevention Functional training Avoid excessive loading until bone strength improves --- 

**14 OSTEOPENIA DEFINITION** Osteopenia is a condition in which bone mineral density is lower than normal but not low enough to meet the diagnostic criteria for osteoporosis For postmenopausal women and men aged 50 years and older a DXA T score between -1 0 and -2 5 is generally classified as osteopenia **CAUSES / RISK FACTORS** Aging Inadequate calcium intake Vitamin D deficiency Physical inactivity Smoking Excessive alcohol Low body weight Menopause Endocrine disorders Long term glucocorticoid therapy Chronic diseases **CLINICAL FEATURES** Usually asymptomatic It may be discovered through bone mineral density testing or evaluation after a fracture **INVESTIGATIONS** DXA scan Main investigation
- T score -1 0 normal
- T score -1 0 to -2 5 osteopenia
- T score -2 5 osteoporosis In younger adults Z scores are generally more appropriate for interpretation **COMPLICATIONS** Progression to osteoporosis Increased fracture risk Vertebral fractures Hip fractures Reduced physical function **MEDICAL MANAGEMENT** Management is based on overall fracture risk not the T score alone Adequate calcium and vitamin D intake Weightbearing exercise Resistance training Smoking cessation Avoid excessive alcohol Fall prevention Treatment of secondary causes Pharmacological therapy for selected patients with sufficiently high
